text: Knowledge management exists to maintain and improve the effective, efficient use of information and knowledge across the organization. Notice the emphasis on use, not volume. A company can own mountains of documentation and still manage knowledge badly if nobody can find the right piece of it at the moment they need it.

ITIL 4 describes how raw material becomes something useful with the DIKW model: data, information, knowledge, wisdom. Data is unprocessed facts — four hundred failed logins at 2 a.m. Information adds context — all from one IP, outside business hours. Knowledge adds experience — this pattern usually means credential stuffing, and here's how we've handled it before.

Wisdom is the top layer: applying that knowledge with judgment to this specific situation, given this organization's risk tolerance, to decide exactly what to do right now. Each layer adds something the one below it couldn't give you on its own.

The practical trap is treating knowledge management as a separate documentation project, with a backlog that grows forever while nobody reads what's already written. ITIL 4 points toward something better: capture knowledge as a byproduct of work already happening — write up a resolved major incident right after the fix, while details are fresh.

The service desk answering the same question for the tenth time is the same opportunity. That tenth answer should become an article the ninety-first caller finds through self-service, with no call needed at all. The technology to store knowledge is rarely the gap most organizations face.

The real obstacle is behavior: will the resolver take two extra minutes to write it up, and will the next person actually search before picking up the phone. Next up: service level management, where you'll set clear targets for how good a service has to be.
